newsitem.title: USA: Clinton doing 'very well' after surgery.
newsitem.headline: Clinton doing 'very well' after surgery.

text.p: President Bill Clinton was described as doing "very well" on Saturday as he recovered from surgery to repair a torn knee tendon and began limited therapy with the aid of the surgeon who operated on him.
Recovering at Bethesda National Naval Medical Centre in suburban Maryland, Clinton was in an upbeat mood, according to those in contact with him.
"He's doing very well ... He's in excellent spirits," said Dr. David Adkinson, the surgeon who performed the operation on Friday and examined his patient on Saturday.

Adkinson said Clinton was resting comfortably and was "focused" on recovering. The physican, based at the naval facility, said Clinton began an early and limited therapy programme -- typical for all patients who have undergone such a procedure.
Adkinson said he slowly moved the president's right knee up and down several times -- a process that will be repeated several times daily during the early stages of Clinton's recovery.
"We'll see where it goes," Adkinson said of Clinton's recovery programme, which he said would be determined by the amount of discomfort the president can tolerate.
"He seems to tolerate (pain) and focus nicely," Adkinson said, adding that Clinton's progress would depend on the discomfort "he can stand."
Dr. Daniel Sewell, who assisted in the operation and visited Clinton on Saturday, also offered a positive assessment. "He's doing great. We're very happy."
Vice President Al Gore, who substituted for Clinton in delivering the president's weekly radio address to the nation, said at the start of his remarks that "the president's doing great."

"He's resting comfortably and he'll be back on his feet, both of them, very soon," said Gore, who noted that Clinton was grateful to "all of you who have sent your prayers and best wishes for a speedy recovery."

Clinton caught his heel on a step at the Florida estate of Australian golfer Greg Norman early on Friday, causing his knee to buckle and tearing the quadriceps tendon connecting the kneecap to the upper thigh in his right leg.
The accident will put Clinton on crutches for about eight weeks, and the president's doctors said it would probably be six months before he could return to his regular running and golf.
White House officials remained upbeat that Clinton would be able to go ahead with plans to meet with Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Helsinki on Wednesday.
A member of the medical team that treated Clinton was expected to accompany him to the summit, along with the physicans that routinely go on a foreign presidential trips.
The accident has forced the postponement of a planned White House visit by Jordan's King Hussein that had been set for Tuesday.

The surgery also led to a delay in the start of a two-week trip to Africa by first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton, who had planned to leave on Saturday. The first lady, who visited the president in the hospital on Saturday, postponed her departure until Sunday to ensure that her husband was all right, aides said.
